name: Priya Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Priya, and thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, how would you describe your work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run Fernlea, a 180-acre tenancy on the county council's farm estate, with about 380 ewes, a few acres of field vegetables for a box scheme, and wheat on the better ground. My partner Omar teaches maths part-time and does the books and the deliveries with me. I've got a farm certificate and twenty-odd years of doing it, and honestly I'm average at the old skills and pretty good at the new ones.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at half five and the first thing I do is check the dashboard on my phone: which ewes' collars show they've stopped grazing, soil moisture in the veg beds, the weather model. Then it's out with the dog, Pip, then the box packing with our three seasonal pickers, Ana, Kasia and Tomasz. I use an AI assistant all day, for rotations, for the box scheme emails, for working out lambing dates. What wears me out is the hand weeding and the lambing nights, and knowing the council could put the rent up at the next review.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was useful but oversold, which is what I've been saying already in the growers' forum. The tools I use now are good, they just don't change the world. I'd say we should get back to talking about land and fair pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, nothing much changes. I'd keep the tools I've got and keep farming. Slightly disappointed, because I was hoping a weeding robot would come down in price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the dashboard and the assistant, maybe try the next version of the drone software. I'd keep putting a bit by each month for when the tenancy comes up for renewal. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a tiny bit bored, if I'm honest. I'd have to find a new thing to be excited about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. In this picture, what do you lose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The dream of a robot that hand-weeds carrots. That's what I really want. If it stays a dream, my back keeps aching every June.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens with Ana, Kasia and Tomasz in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They keep their jobs, which is good, and the hourly rate stays low, which isn't. I'd still be arguing with the other growers about paying pickers properly. That's a fight with or without AI.

S0.say: I'd say AI was useful but oversold, which I already say in the growers' forum. I'd want us back on land and fair pay.
S0.think: For me nothing much changes, I keep my tools and farm on. I'd be slightly disappointed that a weeding robot won't get cheaper.
S0.do: Keeps using the farm dashboard and AI assistant and tries the next drone software update. Keeps saving monthly towards the tenancy renewal.
S0.feel: Calm, a little bored and slightly let down.
S0.quote: If it stays a dream, my back keeps aching every June.
S0.fieldNote: Priya is already a heavy user of AI tools and talks about them like any other piece of kit. Her disappointment is practical: she wants the weeding robot. She turns quickly to pay for her seasonal pickers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let's use it well, and make sure the people doing the hard jobs share the benefits. I'd probably write a long post in the growers' forum about cooperatives owning the kit together, so it's not just the big farms that get it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for me. I'm the kind of farmer who gets the tools first, so I'd be ahead. My bigger worry is the farms around me where people don't want to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go in with two other council tenants and buy a weeding robot together, maybe 40 to 50 thousand split three ways, out of savings. I'd use AI for the box scheme ordering properly. And I'd sit on the county tenants' group to push for a shared machinery fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit excited, honestly. This is the version I'd pick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the weeding robot does arrive, what happens to your pickers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit that sits wrong with me. I'd keep them on for packing and deliveries and pay them better with what we save. But if I'm honest, I'd need fewer of them, maybe two instead of three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you spend, and how much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our share of the robot, maybe 15 thousand, from our savings. The tenancy's the risk, not the money; there's no point owning kit if the council doesn't renew.

S1.say: I'd say let's use it well and make sure people doing the hard jobs share the benefits. I'd write in the growers' forum about cooperatives owning the kit together.
S1.think: I think this is good for me, because I get tools first and I'd be ahead. My bigger worry is neighbours who don't want to change.
S1.do: Buys a weeding robot with two other council tenants, about 15 thousand as her share, from savings. Uses AI for box scheme ordering and pushes the county tenants' group for a shared machinery fund.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, with some guilt about needing fewer pickers.
S1.quote: I'd keep them on for packing and deliveries and pay them better with what we save. But if I'm honest, I'd need fewer of them, maybe two instead of three.
S1.fieldNote: Priya welcomes this picture and moves fast, but through a shared purchase rather than alone, which fits her politics. She's honest about the cost to her pickers. Her real risk is the tenancy, not technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for any democracy to handle and we need public control of these systems now. I'd be on the growers' forum, at the council, writing to everyone. Calm wouldn't be my public face on this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my farm might be fine, I'd buy robots and keep going. But I'd look around at a town with no work and wonder who's buying my veg boxes. And Omar's teaching job would be gone, I'm pretty sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put in for a robot flock and field kit straight away, before everyone else does and prices go up. I'd set aside a year of the pickers' wages to see them through. I'd join the tenants' group pushing for the robots on council land to be publicly owned, and I'd campaign for a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for my money, for everything around it, the school, the shop, the town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very little warning. What does that do to someone who usually moves early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being early doesn't help much when everyone's early. My edge is that I try things first, and here there's no 'first'. It all lands on the same Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Noor and Sami?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Noor's twelve and already asks an AI chat app about her homework. I'd tell her the truth: nobody knows, but we've got the farm and we've got each other. Sami would want to know if a robot can do lambing, and I'd have to say probably yes.

S2.say: I'd say this is too fast for any democracy and we need public control of these systems now. I'd be on the forum and at the council, and I wouldn't pretend to be calm.
S2.think: My farm might be fine because I'd buy robots, but I'd look round a town with no work and wonder who buys my veg boxes. Omar's teaching job would likely go.
S2.do: Orders robot flock and field equipment straight away before prices rise and sets aside a year of pickers' wages. Joins the tenants' group pushing for public ownership of robots on council land and campaigns for a basic income.
S2.feel: Anxious, not about her own money but about the community and customers around her.
S2.quote: My edge is that I try things first, and here there's no 'first'. It all lands on the same Tuesday.
S2.fieldNote: Priya's worry is about the people around her rather than her own job; her adaptability protects her farm but not her customers or her partner's work. She'd move fast on automation while campaigning for public ownership, and she sees no contradiction in that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's build the shared ownership now. I'd run a session at the growers' meeting about it, maybe with the county council there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years is enough for me and the farm. I'd be one of the people setting it up, not having it done to me. My worry is still the people who aren't like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd start a machinery co-op with the other council tenants. Years two and three, I'd add robot weeders, then the shepherding kit, as prices drop. I'd train Ana and Kasia to run and repair them, if they want it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but busy. Busy helps, it always has at lambing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared with two years, what does five change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I can bring people with me instead of just buying in front of them. That's the real difference. Two years is a grab, five is a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be buying robots and campaigning against how they're owned. Is that a contradiction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. But I'd rather the robots are owned by a co-op of small farmers than by the big landowners. If I don't buy, someone with no interest in the valley will.

S3.say: I'd say there are five years, so let's build shared ownership now. I'd run a session at the growers' meeting with the council there.
S3.think: Five years is enough for me and the farm, and I'd be setting it up rather than having it done to me. My worry stays with people who aren't like me.
S3.do: Starts a machinery co-op with other council tenants in the first year and adds robot weeders and shepherding kit as prices fall. Offers to train two pickers to run and repair the machines.
S3.feel: Uneasy but busy, and the busyness helps.
S3.quote: Two years is a grab, five is a plan.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Priya match her politics to her actions: shared ownership and bringing her workers along. She admits the tension between buying robots and criticising ownership, and settles it by preferring a small farmers' co-op. She is calmer when she has something to organise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so let's not waste it on arguing whether it's coming. Plan for a fair version: shared robots, a basic income, land for people who want to grow food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think this is the one where I'm OK. The farm keeps going with robots doing the heavy work, and I'd still do the bits I love, the ewes, the planning, the customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now I'd start the co-op and get the council talking. In a few years I'd turn part of Fernlea into a teaching farm, for school groups and for people who want to learn to grow food once work is gone. And I'd keep pushing politically for a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Even a bit hopeful, which surprises me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. What would you start right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A teaching farm, a co-op, and a lot of meetings. I'd want to be useful, not just comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this that genuinely bothers you, even with all that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That my kids might grow up thinking work is something only machines do. I want Noor and Sami to know how to lamb a ewe, even if they never have to.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift, so don't waste it arguing whether it's coming. Plan for a fair version with shared robots, a basic income and land for people who want to grow food.
S4.think: I think this is the one where I'm OK. Robots do the heavy work and I still do the bits I love, the ewes, the planning and the customers.
S4.do: Starts the machinery co-op and talks to the council now, then turns part of the farm into a teaching farm within a few years. Keeps campaigning for a basic income.
S4.feel: Calm and even a little hopeful, with a quiet worry about what her children will think work is.
S4.quote: I want Noor and Sami to know how to lamb a ewe, even if they never have to.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Priya relaxes and starts imagining a new use for the farm. Her plans are communal: a co-op and a teaching farm. Her only real worry here is cultural, about her children losing a sense of hands-on work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd be fine and nobody around me would be, and that's a horrible feeling. What would help is public ownership of the robots on public land, like council farms, and a basic income in place before it hits, not after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the tenancy. Everyone thinks farmers own their land, but I don't, and if the council decides robots are cheaper than tenants, my whole plan falls over. I've said I'd be fine, but that's the one thing that could make me wrong.

headlineQuote: Everyone thinks farmers own their land, but I don't, and if the council decides robots are cheaper than tenants, my whole plan falls over.
portrait: Priya Haddad is a 43-year-old council tenant farmer who runs Fernlea, a sheep, vegetable and wheat farm, with her partner Omar and three seasonal pickers. She uses AI tools all day and is among the first to try new kit, and she wants the gains shared through co-ops and public ownership. She stays calm in the first two pictures and would buy robots early. AGI by 2028 makes her anxious for her community and her partner rather than herself, while five and ten years let her build a co-op and a teaching farm. Her real weak point is that she doesn't own her land.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she would be fine while the people around her, including her partner, would not.
whatWouldHelp: Public ownership of robots on public land such as council farms, and a basic income in place before AGI arrives.
